messages.author: 5f360b7a2b206a40
messages.subject: Correlation when using same covariate for detection and density
parts:
Hi Everyone,

I am currently working on a project involving using the distsamp function. I am in the process of bootstrapping my best fit models for each year (2018-2022) separately. My study aims to assess the impact of a variety of site (environmental) variables and detection variables. This study is in the alpine and to this end, I have included "distance to snow" as a covariate for both density and detection probabilities in my models. This variable in both the 'detection' and 'abundance' has come up as the best model based on AIC in several of the years.

Upon running the models, I encountered an issue: the output indicates that the covariates for density and detection are highly correlated, exhibiting almost mirror-image coefficients (e.g., density coefficient at 5.891, detection coefficient at -5.77). This raises questions about the interpretability of my model results and the potential confounding effects of using the same environmental covariate for both model components. From an ecological perspective, this makes a lot of sense as this species spends a lot of time foraging on snow and is easily seen (dark bird on white snow), however, the model is showing the opposite. **see output below

Given the structure of unmarkedFrameDS objects, I understand that differentiation between density and detection covariates at the data preparation stage might not be directly feasible. I am reaching out to seek your valuable advice and insights. 

Any guidance on model specification or covariate selection that might help mitigate this issue would be greatly appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Correlation when using same covariate for detection and density
parts:
Hi Tim,

what you say, and also the high absolute values of the estimated coefficients for snow, don't look so good to me. In principle, in these types of hierarchical models separate effects of a covariate on both the state and the observation models should be estimable. However, sometimes, due to the particularities of a specific data set, they may be not.

What happens if you build up the model in simple steps, from one having only an intercept in each part and then up to the model you have now ? How do the estimates for snow change along this progression ?

Best regards  --- Marc

I'm encountering a similar problem in the field, which I've been pondering ahead of trying to parameterize or run updated occupancy or N-mix models.  We're in our 7th year of surveying vernal pools for amphibian egg masses.  All field staff agree that there's been an increase in filamentous algae over the last 2-3 yrs which seems to obviously reduce detection.  Does the algae also depress occupancy or abundance?  We have a priori (biological) reason to think so.  But if detection declines strongly and consistently across all observers with increasing algal cover, can the models detect a change in the state variable on top of a detection decline?  Seems like another potential 'perfectly confounding' variable as Matt called it.

-Alex

messages.author: 5f360b7a2b206a40
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Correlation when using same covariate for detection and density
parts:
Hi Marc (et. al),

Thank you for your guidance! Your suggestion to build the model incrementally has been very insightful, helping to pinpoint where the estimates for snow covariates begin to diverge in expected ways. In the field, our measurements included 'snow cover' at each site (50m radius, along with other cover estimates up to 100% (exposed rock, bare ground, woody very, graminoids, forbs, etc), which I'm now considering as a proxy for snow frequency in the detection model. This seems ecologically valid as the presence and extent of 'snow cover' should influence visibility and detection probability for a dark bird on white snow. In our models, the 'distance to snow' covariate is ecologically relevant for density, as we see increased bird densities closer to snow. This aligns with our field data, showing that detections are more frequent near snow, highlighting the ecological importance of snow for these birds.

I've also generated a histogram of counts as a function of the 'distance to snow' covariate. Interestingly, the results align with our field observations and annual variations in snowpack. For example, 2019 had a high snow year and most sites had snow within ~50m, while 2022, a low snow year, had sites with snow typically >50m away.

Despite this ecological rationale, the mirrored coefficients for snow in the density and detection equations are causing some confusion. It seems counterintuitive since higher bird densities near snow should also lead to higher detection probabilities, not lower. This points to a potential confounding effect within the model and is why I have reached out to the unmarked group.

These are good points. In the field, we took measurements for snow, distance to snow (snowpatch of a minimum size) and snow as a percent cover at each site in a 50m radius, along with other cover estimates up to 100% (exposed rock, bare ground, woody very, graminoids, forbs, etc). We had detections from 1-200m of our target species with a truncation of 170m. distance to snow, distance to cliffs - independently, but even more so as an interaction term (co-limiting) were highly significant with density. These species spend a great deal of time on the snow, and like I mentioned, seeing a dark bird on white snow makes detection highly precise, even up to longer distances. 

I will continue with the incremental model-building approach and consider additional covariates that might better differentiate the effects on density and detection. Any further thoughts on this matter, or suggestions for disentangling these intertwined effects, would be greatly appreciated!

Best,
Tim

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: AW: [unmarked] Correlation when using same covariate for detection and density
parts:
Dear all,

 

ever since this paper I have known that in principle we can separate the effects of a covariate on the state and the observation parts of a hierarchical model (and surely other people have shown this before ---- there is rarely something new under the sun). I wouldn’t be surprised if there are situations where the model breaks when a single covariate has effects on both parts of the model, but I’d be interested to see someone identifying these conditions in a controlled simulation study.

 

As a small part in another modeling project, with what we call an integrated distance sampling model, we have just repeated such a type of simulation, where the same covariate affected both components of the model, and things worked just wonderfully (this is Simulation 2 in the paper).

 

Best regards  -- Marc
